entities.name: Statute of the International Court of Justice
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Statute of the International Court of Justice (ICJ), adopted on April 29, 1945, during the United Nations Conference on International Organization in San Francisco, serves as the foundational legal document establishing the ICJ's framework and operational guidelines. The ICJ, located in The Hague, Netherlands, is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations and plays a crucial role in resolving disputes between states and providing advisory opinions on international legal issues. The creation of the ICJ marked a significant step in the evolution of international law and diplomacy, aiming to promote peace and security after the catastrophic impacts of World War II.

The Statute outlines the jurisdiction, procedures, and functions of the Court, which hears cases brought by states and issues advisory opinions on legal questions referred to it by the UN General Assembly and Security Council. With 15 judges elected for nine-year terms, the Court's deliberations are based on principles of justice and international law, drawing upon treaties, customary law, and judicial decisions. Its first case was adjudicated in 1947, setting precedents for future international legal proceedings and enhancing the role of the judiciary in global governance.

The legacy of the Statute is profound, as it has established a framework that has been referenced in numerous international treaties and legal instruments, fostering a culture of compliance with international law among nations. The ICJ's decisions have influenced various global conflicts, such as the territorial disputes in the South China Sea and the legality of the use of force, thus shaping the international legal landscape. This legal institution has also inspired the creation of other international courts and tribunals, contributing to a more structured approach to international dispute resolution and human rights enforcement.
